patient_actor_hidden.History: The patient reports a 6-week history of tingling pain in the sole of his right foot, which worsens when he raises it above chest level during exercises. He mentions that he began exercising regularly 2 months ago and experiences right calf cramps with the use of the treadmill's incline feature, necessitating frequent breaks. The pain subsides completely after a few minutes of resting. He adds an 8-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Symptoms.Primary_Symptom: Tingling pain in the sole of the right foot upon elevation

patient_actor_hidden.Social_History: Smokes two packs of cigarettes daily for 34 years.

objective_for_doctor: Assess and diagnose the patient presenting with tingling pain in the sole of the right foot, especially upon elevation and during exercise, with a significant history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and smoking.

turns.content: Hello, I'm your doctor today. What brings you in today?

Doctor: Hello, I’m your doctor today. What brings you in today? Patient: I’ve had about six weeks of tingling pain in the sole of my right foot, especially when I raise it during exercise, and it completely goes away after I rest for a few minutes. I also get cramping in my right calf when I use the treadmill incline, so I have to stop frequently.
Do you have a history of smoking, diabetes, high blood pressure, or high cholesterol?
Patient: Yes—I've had type 2 diabetes for about 8 years, and I also smoke about two packs a day for 34 years. I don’t know of any diagnosed high blood pressure or high cholesterol.
When the cramping or tingling begins, does it resolve if you simply stop and stand still, or do you need to sit down or lean forward to feel better?
Patient: If I stop and just stand still, it eases within a few minutes, and the tingling goes away—I don’t have to sit down or lean forward.
Have you noticed any skin changes on your right leg or foot, such as coolness, paleness, hair loss, or slow-healing sores?

Patient: I haven’t noticed any coolness or paleness, and there’s been no hair loss or slow-healing sores on the right foot or leg. The symptoms mainly show up during exercise and then improve within a few minutes of stopping.
Have you or a clinician ever noted weak or absent pulses in your right foot or ankle compared to the left?

Patient: I haven’t specifically checked or been told that my right ankle or foot pulses are weaker than the left, so I’m not sure. If you examine them, I can tell you what I’ve noticed day to day, but I haven’t noticed a clear difference myself.
Do you ever experience pain, tingling, or cramping in your right leg or foot while resting or sleeping at night?
Patient: No, it doesn’t really happen when I’m resting or sleeping—most of it comes on with exercise, and once I stop it eases within a few minutes.

[DDX] Peripheral artery disease (intermittent claudication), Lumbar spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication), Diabetic peripheral neuropathy, Chronic exertional compartment syndrome, Tarsal tunnel syndrome
